title: Google has Gemini 4 agents meet to revamp quantum algorithms: up to 290x speedup, with a mathematical proof of correctness

content_html:
Quantum computing's most awkward predicament right now is that there are capable problems but no suitable algorithms to feed them—even with today's best quantum algorithms, some truly important applications require resources far beyond what early quantum hardware can support. In a new study released jointly by the Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI teams on November 23, they offered a new approach: having multiple Gemini 4 agents work together to optimize classic quantum algorithms and generate quantum circuits with striking efficiency.

Quantum circuits are the instruction sets by which quantum computers execute algorithms. The more streamlined the circuit, the fewer qubits and operations a machine needs to do the same work. The scenarios reworked by the agents in their "meeting" this time were several aimed at major human challenges. For calculating key properties of inertial confinement fusion—the fusion route that uses lasers to compress hydrogen fuel to ignition—the team found corresponding quantum circuits that cut the overall compute cost by 11.8x and reduced the number of error-corrected qubits required from 5,650 to 4,338. Drug design was also put on the ledger: for common photosensitive molecules, quantum simulation costs fell by 8x, and the logic by which the algorithm tracks particle positions and electric-field forces was simplified; for cytochrome P450 enzymes, which break down most drugs in the human body and are crucial to pharmaceuticals, the team achieved a 2.5x performance gain by replacing redundant memory lookup operations, reducing memory usage from 481 qubits to 333. There were gains at the basic-algorithm level as well: a specific implementation of Grover's algorithm for searching unsorted lists sped up by 2.57x, and an arcsine (arcsin) subroutine responsible for loading data into quantum states sped up by up to 290x.

The hardest part of this pipeline is "proof." Resource-intensive quantum circuits cannot be tested directly on classical computers or today's small-scale quantum processors, so the team had to take another path—mathematically proving their correctness. Every optimization result was mathematically verified by the agent team using the formal theorem prover Lean. To let the research community reuse it directly, the team has open-sourced the relevant Lean libraries, problem-definition files, and verified solutions on GitHub, essentially handing over a quantum algorithm workbench with correctness guarantees.

A new division of labor is also emerging. In this process, researchers need to set the research direction, define the problems, monitor the agents' progress, and feed in their own expertise in quantum algorithms; scientific results were produced through this collaborative "meeting" process. This proof-verified AI search process drastically compresses manual design work that once took years, freeing humans to focus on selecting problems and interpreting results.

Of course, Google did not overstate its case. Even after these optimizations, actually running these algorithms in scientific simulation scenarios would still require computing power beyond the capabilities of first-generation error-corrected quantum computers. But the value of these improvements is already clear—AI has moved fusion energy and drug design, hard problems bottlenecked by computing power, one step closer to the day when quantum hardware can reach them.
